name: OECD.AI Policy Observatory: Tracking National AI Strategies and Public-Sector AI
title: OECD.AI Policy Observatory: Tracking National AI Strategies and Public-Sector AI
answer: OECD.AI is the OECD's public observatory on artificial intelligence policy, publishing blog posts and research on national AI strategies, trustworthy AI tools, classification frameworks and government AI funding. Its most useful contribution for government readers is the OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems, which lets policymakers sort AI systems by autonomy, sector, data use and impact so they can assess risk, monitor bias and manage inventories of systems in public use.

sections.body: OECD.AI is the online policy observatory of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the Paris-based intergovernmental body. The pages read are a mix of blog posts, news items and research summaries published under the oecd.ai domain, covering national AI strategies, ethical frameworks, expert networks and measurement of government AI research and development. The material is dated mainly to 2019, 2020 and 2021, with references to the OECD AI Principles adopted in May 2019 and to a public consultation held in June 2021. It is written for policymakers, officials and analysts rather than for a general audience.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The observatory's central subject is how governments organise themselves around AI. Several posts describe national strategies: the American AI Initiative launched by Executive Order 13859 on 11 February 2019, which the site says aligns with the OECD AI Principles, and Singapore's Model Governance Framework, described as sector and technology agnostic and built on two guiding principles, that AI-assisted decision making should be explainable, transparent and fair, and that ethical principles should be translated into implementable practices. Other posts describe the OECD's own machinery. The Network of Experts on AI, chaired in 2020 by Adam Murray of the U.S. Department of State, advises the OECD Committee on Digital Economy Policy and had over 70 members nominated by the OECD's 37 member countries, the European Commission and four stakeholder groups, with observers from UNESCO, the Council of Europe, the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank. A working group on implementing trustworthy AI has built a comparative framework and a live database of tools, ranging from bias-detection software to procedural guidelines and training initiatives. The OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems helps policymakers classify systems by autonomy, sector, data collection and impact, with a People and Planet dimension placed at the centre after public consultation. A study with Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology tested whether such frameworks guide users to consistent classifications. A separate OECD study measures the AI content of government-funded R&D projects by scanning project abstracts for AI-related terms.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The OECD AI Principles were adopted in May 2019 and define a system as trustworthy if it promotes inclusive growth, human-centred values, transparency, safety and security, and accountability. ONE AI had over 70 members in 2020, nominated by 37 member countries plus the European Commission and four stakeholder groups. The working group analysed over 75 submissions, in a sentence truncated on the page. The classification framework's People and Planet dimension was elevated after a public consultation in June 2021. The American AI Initiative was launched on 11 February 2019 by Executive Order 13859, and President Trump proposed a two-year doubling of non-defence AI R&D in the fiscal year 2021 budget. The German AI Observatory began in March 2020. One blog describes an industrial equipment company with 750 employees and 100 million Euros in revenue.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in government, this source is a map of the policy landscape rather than a news feed. It gathers national strategies, ethical frameworks and expert networks in one place, and it offers practical instruments: a classification framework that public bodies can use to inventory and risk-assess the AI systems they deploy, a database of tools for building trustworthy systems, and a method for measuring how much government R&D money actually goes to AI. Officials drafting procurement rules, setting up oversight registers or comparing their country's approach with others will find the comparative material and the definitions of trustworthiness directly usable.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Government

sections.body: The pages are largely dated to 2019 to 2021, so they describe strategies and networks as they stood then, not current positions. Several sentences are truncated, including the reference to over 75 analysed submissions and a NIST announcement, so some detail is incomplete. The material is explanatory and promotional of OECD instruments rather than critical, and it does not provide operational guidance for building or procuring specific systems. Coverage is weighted towards OECD member and partner countries, and the blog format means individual posts vary in depth.
